name: thank_you_cards
description: One row per printed card. user_id is indexed rather than unique: blocking a card creates the plural by itself, because a blocked card is kept rather than deleted.

columns.name: code
columns.description: 'DK-' plus 32 hex characters: 16 fully random bytes, no timestamp. Length inside a QR code is free, so there is no reason to spend part of it on the creation time the way transaction links do.

columns.name: label
columns.description: The member's own word for the card. It is printed on it, so the till that scans it shows it back — never a secret from whoever holds the card, and never reaching anybody else.

columns.name: failed_attempts
columns.description: Counted on the card, not on the person: once more than one card may be valid, guessing at one must not block the other.

columns.name: blocked_at
columns.description: NULL means usable. Blocking is reversible; deleting is not, which is why blocking is what exists.

notes: Never delete a row here. A kept row is what lets a scan of an old card answer 'this card is blocked' instead of running into nothing, and what lets an old receipt still name the card a payment was made with. transactions.thank_you_card_id points at it.

code is a bearer secret in the sense that whoever scans it can ask for a payment — but not authorise one, which needs the PIN. It must not be logged and must not be returned for a card the caller does not own.

failed_attempts is reset to 0 on a successful payment, and reaching THANK_YOU_CARD_MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS is what sets blocked_at. The counter is incremented by the database (failed_attempts + 1), not by reading and writing back — two tills guessing at once must not lose a count.

Blocking an already blocked card does not move blocked_at forward: the moment a card died is worth keeping. Unblocking clears blocked_at and resets failed_attempts together — one without the other leaves a usable card one wrong PIN from dying again.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.
